transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Well… it’s the bridges, doctor. Crossing them, I mean. Or even knowing I’m going to have to cross one. If I’m in the car and it becomes clear there’s no way around it, it starts before we even get onto the bridge. My heart begins pounding very hard, my hands get damp—on the steering wheel if I’m driving, or gripping the armrest if I’m not—and I get this awful rush of fear, just all at once. It’s not a mild nervousness. It hits me immediately, like my body has decided something terrible is about to happen before I’ve even reached the bridge.
Do these sudden rushes of fear ever happen when you’re not facing a bridge or thinking about crossing one?

No… not really in the same way. It’s very tied to the bridge, or to realizing I’m going to have to cross one. The moment it becomes unavoidable—like if I can see the route is taking me there, or there’s no way to turn off—then it starts. My heart begins pounding, my hands get damp, whether they’re on the steering wheel or I’m just clutching the armrest, and I get that awful rush of fear before I’m even actually on the bridge.

But just sitting at home, or going about the day, I don’t get that sudden surge out of nowhere. It’s when the bridge is coming, or I know it’s coming.
Do you get this same fear in other situations where it might be hard to leave quickly, like tunnels or being far from an exit?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way, no. I mean… tunnels aren’t pleasant, exactly, and at my age I don’t love feeling boxed in anywhere, but I haven’t noticed that same kind of sudden fear just because it would be hard to get out quickly.

It’s really when there’s a bridge involved that my mind seems to lock onto it. If you’re asking whether I panic in all trapped situations—like being far from an exit, or in a tunnel, or something like that—I don’t think so. At least, not in the same way. I haven’t paid close attention to every situation, but the thing that stands out, the thing that really sets me off, is the bridge.
When you’re about to cross a bridge, is your fear mainly that you wouldn’t be able to get away or get help if you needed to?

No… I don’t think that’s the main thing. I mean, I suppose being stuck up there would be awful, of course, but when I really look at what flashes through my mind, it’s more… the bridge itself. The height, the span, the idea of it giving way.

I know perfectly well, rationally, that thousands and thousands of cars go over those bridges every day and nothing happens. I can say that sitting here. I’m not foolish; I understand they’re built to hold traffic. But when I see a high bridge on the map, or worse, when it comes into view through the windshield, it’s as if all that common sense just drops away. It feels like the whole thing is waiting to drop out from under us. Like the road won’t be there anymore.

So no, it’s not mainly, “What if I can’t get help?” It’s more, “What if this bridge doesn’t hold?” Even saying it sounds unreasonable, but that’s what it feels like in the moment.
Do you avoid crossing bridges whenever you can?

Yes. Very much so. I mean, I don’t just “prefer” not to cross them—I plan around them now.

For more than two years, I’ve been arranging errands and visits so I don’t have to go over bridges if there’s any possible alternative. I’ll look at the map ahead of time, sometimes more than once, and if I see that a route takes me over a bridge, especially a high one, I start trying to find another way around. Even if it adds a ridiculous amount of time, I’ll take the longer way if it means staying on regular roads.

I’ve given up trips because of it. I used to enjoy going to San Juan, and I’ve stopped doing that. Seattle theater nights too—those were something I liked, and now I just don’t go, because the bridge part becomes the whole thing in my mind. It’s not worth the dread leading up to it.

And if I absolutely have to cross one, I can’t just do it casually. I need the route studied beforehand, I need to know exactly when it’s coming, I prefer the timing to be just so—traffic, daylight, all of that—and I need someone with me. Even then I’m frightened the whole way across. I just sit there trying to get through it until we’re off the bridge.
